1.pericope_label: The second tables hewn and carried up

schools.summary: Calvin holds that God would leave some trace of the punishment behind, like a scar remaining after the wound has healed, the people being humbled by this one mark, that the stones which carried the covenant were not fashioned by his hand nor quarried from the sacred mount; he will not guess why no witness was admitted, but sees what the arrangement gained, since God left room for faith by using a man's hand, and the proof stood anyway, the people having watched Moses carry the tables up blank. Gill reads the exclusion as discipline, those who had sinned in the calf being shut out and Joshua with them.

Henry turns the change into a history of revelation: when the law was first written on the heart of man both tables and writing were God's work, and only when that was broken did God take up the ministry of men, the prophets and apostles hewing the tables while the writing stayed his own; he notes that God did not alter his measures although the last long absence had produced the calf, and that Moses rose early, the morning being as good a friend to the graces as it is to the muses.

Clarke faces the apparent contradiction between this chapter and Deuteronomy over who wrote the second tables, and answers it by distinguishing two documents, God engraving the commandments on the tables laid up in the ark while Moses wrote a copy for the congregation, authenticated under God's direction; Wesley follows Henry closely.

Ellicott puts the loss as a maxim, that something is always lost by sin even when it is forgiven, insists the second tables were inscribed by the finger of God as the first were, and marks how new the stringency of the solitude was, connecting it with the glory Moses had been promised he should see; Keil and Delitzsch explain the change from tables of stone to tables of stones by the plain fact that Moses cut his from two separate blocks.

debates.question: Who wrote the words on the second tables?

sides.position: God, exactly as on the first — the idiom permits it and Deuteronomy requires it
both, of different documents — God the tables laid up in the ark, Moses the copy given to the people

themes: hew thee two tables of stone
I will write upon these tables
no man shall come up with thee
Moses rose up early in the morning

schools.summary: Calvin says the people watched the cloud take Moses into it, so that after forty days out of the common life of men he might come forth like a new man, warns against pressing the word descended since God fills heaven and earth and does not shift his position, and allows that the phrase about calling on the name may be read either of God proclaiming his own titles or of Moses professing his piety; Gill identifies the cloud with the pillar that had gone before Israel.

Henry reads the descent as condescension, God humbling himself to notice a man who had humbled himself to walk with him, and thinks the cloud was meant to keep awe alive lest familiarity breed contempt; he notes the proclamation was made in passing and draws a rule from it, that fixed views of God are reserved for the future state, sets the disclosure at the bush against this one as self-existence against grace, and insists that greatness and goodness set each other off, since we are told how good God is lest his greatness make us afraid and how great he is lest we presume on his goodness.
Wesley identifies the cloud with the same pillar that had met Moses at the tent door the day before.

Ellicott follows the cloud's movement closely, since it withdrew from the tent door when Moses left off communing there and seemed to vanish, then became visible again at the summit and came down where he stood.

themes: the Lord descended in the cloud
stood with him there
proclaimed the name of the Lord
merciful and gracious, longsuffering

schools.summary: Gill finds the largeness of the grace written into the page itself, reporting that the first letter of the word for keeping is drawn longer than usual in the Hebrew text, which the Jews took for a sign of how far this mercy extends.

Clarke treats the verse as God's own definition of his name, is impatient with the long history of guessing at it — some holding it inexplicable, some parcelling its letters among the persons of the Trinity — and asks how strange it is that none of these learned men noticed that God interprets it here himself; he then counts eleven titles and glosses each, and sets the versions of the closing clause side by side, the Samaritan changing one letter to get with whom the innocent shall be innocent, the Vulgate paraphrasing it that no man is innocent of himself before God. Wesley dwells on the abundance, that there is mercy enough for all, enough for each, enough for ever, and narrows the last clause to the impenitently guilty.

Ellicott says this new name is not a name as we use the word but a description by accumulated epithets, arranges the three great disclosures in order — self-existence at the bush, terribleness in the descent on Sinai, mercy in the act of pardoning — and gives the reason the clause about the guilty is there at all, to prevent the fatal misapprehension that God is a being of pure and mere benevolence.

debates.question: How should the clause about not clearing the guilty be rendered?

sides.position: the versions differ widely — the Samaritan gives with whom the innocent shall be innocent, the Vulgate that no man is innocent of himself
it means the impenitently guilty, and those who would be cleared without satisfaction to justice

themes: abundant in goodness and truth
keeping mercy for thousands
forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin
that will by no means clear the guilty

schools.summary: Calvin reads the haste as astonishment, since God when he reveals himself so ravishes the godly with admiration that they have no leisure to deliberate but are struck down at once, and takes the last petition causally, as though God could not enjoy the inheritance he had chosen except by pardoning their sins — which he applies beyond that generation, our own progress in grace being nothing but a continual reconciling. Gill has Moses hurry because he perceived the voice ceasing and feared to lose the opportunity, and reads the opening words as certainty rather than doubt.

Clarke observes that the title Moses uses here is not Jehovah but Adonai, which he takes to point to the Angel of the Covenant; Wesley states the paradox of the plea, that God had given their stiff neck as his reason for not going with them and Moses answers that the worse they are the more they need him, and notes that the whole prayer asks for nothing God had not already promised, Moses praying not from doubt of the grant but from anxiety to have it ratified.

Ellicott admires the combination in him, an ardent desire to look into the things of God joined with a reverence that would not look until the glory had gone by, lists what was asked, and notes that no direct answer is given to any of it, the prayer being accepted indirectly by the renewal of the covenant.

themes: Moses made haste and bowed his head
let my Lord go among us
it is a stiffnecked people
take us for thine inheritance

10.pericope_label: The covenant renewed and the leagues forbidden

schools.summary: Calvin notes that the text does not say with whom the covenant is made and thinks the sense the same either way, since Moses stipulated for all; on the leagues he grants that the command to destroy cannot be pressed on us as it stood, since God does not now bid us put the wicked to death, yet insists the case has reference to us, and draws the distinction that we cannot escape the ordinary dealings of life with unbelievers without going out of the world, while closer ties open the door to Satan. Gill points out that the caution is addressed not to Moses but to the people, against the day they should possess the land.

Henry marks who is speaking, since when the covenant was broken it was Israel that broke it and now that it is renewed it is God who makes it, so that if there are quarrels we bear all the blame and if there is peace God has all the glory; he treats the two great precepts as fences round each other and presses the reasonableness of the ban, that if God makes war with the Canaanites Israel should not make peace with them, adding that such is the corruption of nature that the bad are likelier to debauch the good than the good to reform the bad.
Clarke and Wesley both read the promised marvels forward into Joshua, the drying up of Jordan, the fall of Jericho and the sun standing still.

Ellicott spells out the terms as a bargain on both sides and notes that the command given takes in the ten words and a summary of the older book of the covenant, which is thereby republished; Keil and Delitzsch describe the structure, the Lord repeating two leading points which are the main pillars meant to carry the renewed covenant.

themes: behold, I make a covenant
I will do marvels
make no covenant with the inhabitants
ye shall destroy their altars

14.pericope_label: Jealousy, molten gods, and the feasts

schools.summary: Calvin takes the prohibition to its root, since when statues and pictures are called gods the sum of the second commandment appears, that God is insulted when he is clothed in a corporeal image; he is careful about what the heathen actually believed, that they did not suppose the deity shut up in matter but imagined it nearer if some earthly symbol stood before their eyes, and notes that gold is no more abominable to God than wood, molten gods being condemned by name because superstition is the more inflamed by a costly material. Gill reads the word as a part standing for the whole, though he thinks molten images named because the calf had been one.

Henry sees why the feasts are repeated here, since the people had proclaimed a feast in honour of the calf and are now charged with keeping the feasts God appointed; he draws the lesson that nobody need be drawn from religion by the promise of mirth, presses the weekly rest in its hardest case, that it holds in ploughing and harvest and that harvest will prosper the better for it, and answers the objection that a country emptied of its men three times a year lay open, since God can restrain not only men's actions but their wishes.

Ellicott defends the divine jealousy against those who find it unworthy of God, since indifference to idolatry would mean he cared little for his creatures, like the god of Epicurus who having once made the world paid it no attention, and suggests that the makers of the calf may have supposed themselves clear of a commandment forbidding only graven images; Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole calendar in order.

themes: the Lord, whose name is Jealous
thou shalt make thee no molten gods
the feast of unleavened bread
neither shall any man desire thy land

21.pericope_label: The sabbath in harvest and the three appearances

schools.summary: Gill notes that the law of the seventh day is repeated here to fix it in their minds, takes the first of the appended rules to mean that the passover was not to be killed while any leaven remained in the houses, and does no more with the last two than point back to where they stood before.

Clarke presses the temptation the verse is aimed at, since many break the sabbath on a plea of necessity, reckoning that if the weather has been bad through harvest and the sabbath comes fine, the fineness of the day is a providential indication that it should be used — and he adds that he has known the law often broken on that pretence and never found such men prosper one whit better than their more conscientious neighbours; on the three appearances he treats the safety of the emptied country as a standing proof of the divine origin of the religion and a barrier no deistical mind can get over. Wesley says the people were kept not merely from invading but from so much as thinking of it.

Ellicott observes how often the sabbath law comes round in this book, appearing in every section of the legislation, glosses earing time as ploughing time from an old English verb, finds a partial parallel to the festival truce in the unwritten law of the Greeks though the promise here goes far beyond it, and traces a double promise and a double fulfilment in the enlarging of the borders.

themes: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest
thrice in the year shall all your men children appear
I will enlarge thy borders
the firstfruits and the kid

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the number had to be the same, since a stay of a few days would not have ratified Moses' authority by any conspicuous miracle, and is careful about the kind of fast it was — no fast of temperance but a special privilege, an exemption from the infirmity of the flesh, so that he felt no hunger and wanted food no more than an angel; from this he turns on the annual fast of the Church as a gross error, men setting themselves to rival the Son of God as though a new promulgation of the gospel had been entrusted to them. Gill reckons this a third period of forty days rather than a repetition of the first.

Henry reads the forty days as communion rather than endurance, since Moses did not think it long, and gives two reasons why he needed nothing, that the power of God supported him and that his communion with God entertained him, so that he had meat to eat which the world knew not of; he adds one comparison that keeps the honour in proportion, that our Lord's face shone as the sun and his clothing with it, yet coming down from his mountain he laid that glory aside.

Ellicott finds the length surprising at first sight, there being no fresh instructions to give, and takes the answer from Deuteronomy, that the time went in a long intercession which at last prevailed; he notes that fasts of this duration are recorded only of Moses, Elijah and our Lord, and insists with Keil and Delitzsch that the subject of the verb wrote is God and not Moses, the Hebrew idiom permitting it and the rest of Scripture requiring it.

themes: forty days and forty nights
he did neither eat bread nor drink water
he wrote upon the tables
the words of the covenant

schools.summary: Calvin thinks the shining was hidden from Moses for a time on purpose, so that he might come down freely and the miracle be the more evident when seen close at hand, and turns the people's fear into a rebuke, since they were branded with that mark of disgrace to make them confess how far their ingratitude had carried them from God, Moses coming down securely from speaking with him while they shrank from the sight of a mortal. Gill limits who saw it to the princes who met him at the foot of the mountain.

Clarke makes the most of the strange verb, which means to send out horns and so is used of rays darting from a polished surface, blames the Latin version for the horned face and asks why the painters gave him only two, and traces the halo of art to this verse; on the people's fear he says the sight alarmed them because their consciences were still guilty and they had not yet received the atonement. Wesley takes the shining as an honour done to the man, so that his mission might never be questioned again, and thinks the people could not tell whether the light was a token of favour or of displeasure.

Ellicott insists the phenomenon was physical and not figurative, reports the view that such radiance once belonged to man as part of the image of God and is restored now and then to particular saints, and would render the phrase not while he talked with him but through his talking with him; Keil and Delitzsch state the fact simply, that the sight of the glory, though only of its reflection, so wrought on the skin of his face that it shone without his observing it.

themes: the skin of his face shone
Moses wist not that it shone
they were afraid to come nigh him
the horns of the Vulgate

schools.summary: Gill takes our version as it stands and will not have the Greek reading that Moses veiled himself when he had finished, since on that reading there would have been no occasion for the veil at all; he holds that Moses covered his face as soon as he perceived the glory the people could not bear, and notes at the close that nobody can say how long the shining lasted, though one rabbi held it never left him to the day of his death.

Clarke builds the whole contrast of the two dispensations on the veil, since as the glory of Moses' face was swallowed up in the splendour of God when he entered the tabernacle, so the brightness of the law is eclipsed by the gospel — the one showing sin in its exceeding sinfulness but making no provision for pardon, the other exhibiting the Lamb of God putting away sin by the sacrifice of himself; he reads the veil twice over as a figure, of the ceremonies each covering a spiritual meaning and of the darkness that came on the nation, and finds a survival of it in the tasselled cloth a Jew still draws over his head to read the law. Wesley reads it as the darkness of that dispensation, beauty veiled, gold in the mine, a pearl in the shell.

Ellicott says flatly that the English exactly inverts the sense, the veil going on when the speaking was over; on his reading it became part of Moses' ordinary dress, laid aside only when he went in alone to God and when he came out with a message, which he authenticated by uncovering and letting the brightness be seen.

debates.question: When did Moses put the veil on?

sides.position: while he spoke, as soon as he saw the people could not bear the brightness — the Greek reading leaves no occasion for a veil at all
when the speaking was over; the English rendering exactly inverts the sense

themes: he put a vail on his face
when he went in before the Lord he took it off
the veil and the two dispensations
how long the shining lasted
